paragraphs: Defenders of federal constitutions have usually rested their case on a geography of trust: authority exercised by a provincial legislature, they argue, benefits from the propinquity of rulers and ruled, who share local knowledge that a distant capital lacks. The standard objection, which James Madison pressed against the champions of small republics, is that propinquity also breeds faction; a compact polity is easily captured by a single interest, and its quarrels tend to be internecine precisely because everyone knows everyone else. Madison's answer was to treat the scale of the union, rather than the virtue of its parts, as the safeguard.

A more recent school of political theorists holds that neither local trust nor continental scale explains why federations endure. What holds them together, on this view, is not the formal demarcation of powers in a constitutional text, which courts enforce only sporadically, but political parties that operate at both levels and so mediate between them: a national politician who depends on provincial organizations has every reason to respect provincial prerogatives. The thesis has real explanatory merit, since it accounts for the otherwise puzzling durability of federations whose courts almost never strike down a national statute. Yet it is curiously silent about the converse case. A party disciplined enough to carry provincial interests into the capital is disciplined enough to carry the capital's instructions back to the provinces, and where a single such party dominates, the formal autonomy of the provinces can be nullified without a single amendment being passed. The political safeguards of federalism, in other words, work only so long as party competition remains factious enough that no one organization commands both levels at once.

The lightest elements are primordial: hydrogen, helium and a trace of lithium emerged from the first minutes after the Big Bang. Nearly everything heavier was forged later, in stars, but fusion can carry a star only as far as iron, beyond which building heavier nuclei consumes energy rather than releasing it. The heavier elements must therefore be assembled by neutron capture. In the slow process, nuclei inside aging giant stars absorb neutrons one at a time over thousands of years, each capture followed by radioactive decay before the next arrives. The rapid process, which yields much of the universe's gold and uranium, requires a flood of neutrons so dense that nuclei swell faster than they can decay, and for decades its site was a matter of conjecture. The 2017 detection of gravitational waves from two merging neutron stars, followed by light whose colors bore the palpable signature of freshly made heavy elements, settled that such mergers produce rapid-process elements; whether they produce enough of them, early enough in cosmic history, remains open, and the unexpectedly gold-rich atmospheres of some very old stars may portend a second site not yet identified.

To cut costs, the Pell County transit authority plans to replace each of its diesel buses with an electric bus as the diesel wears out. An electric bus costs more to buy, but the authority calculates that its lower fuel and maintenance costs will more than make up the difference over the twelve years a bus typically stays in service. The authority concludes that the plan will reduce its costs.

For much of the twentieth century, literary historians treated the Spanish picaresque novel as an apprenticeship that European fiction had to outgrow. Lazarillo de Tormes (1554) and its successors were credited with irreverent energy, with an insouciant low-born narrator who cozens his way from master to master, and with a satirical survey of a society whose priests, nobles and officials prove no more honest than he; but they were faulted for their form. The episodes follow one another without development, the hero learns tricks rather than wisdom, and the book could end almost anywhere. On this account the picaresque supplied the realist novel with its subject, the ordinary and the poor, while leaving to later writers the task of giving that subject a shape.

Revisionist critics have interrogated that verdict, arguing that the charge of formlessness misreads a form. A life lived from one meal to the next, they contend, cannot be narrated as a career; the string of separate episodes is mimetic of a precariousness in which no plan survives the next change of master, and to demand development of such a book is to demand that its hero be someone other than poor. This defense has the merit of taking the books' structure seriously, and it disposes of the assumption that episodic narrative is merely a failure to achieve plot. But it purchases coherence for the episodes by denying them a designer. The picaresque narrator is not only the hero of his adventures but their retrospective teller, and he tells them to someone: Lazarillo addresses an unnamed person of rank who has asked for an account of a scandal touching the narrator's household. Read in that light, the episodes are not a passive record of what poverty did to a boy but a selection of evidence, arranged to show that a man so schooled could hardly have acted otherwise. The form of the early picaresque is less mimetic than forensic; its apparent artlessness is the artfulness of a defendant.

It was once a commonplace that the mechanical clock was a monastic invention. The Benedictine rule divided the day among offices of prayer, and historians from Lewis Mumford onward took the monastery, with its bells and its regimented hours, as the paradigmatic setting in which Europeans first learned to live by the clock. The documentary record tells a different story. The earliest weight-driven clocks, which appeared around 1300, drifted by a quarter of an hour or more a day and had to be reset against a sundial; they could hardly have improved on a bell-ringer's judgment, and monastic sources rarely mention them. Where they appear in abundance is in the towers of Italian and Flemish towns, whose councils, clamorous rivals in most things, competed to pay for machines that announced the hours with a clangor audible across the whole commune.

The difference was not merely one of location; it was, in a sense, metaphysical. The monastic hours were unequal: the offices were fixed by sunrise and sunset, so that an hour of a summer day was far longer than an hour of a winter one. The town clock, by contrast, struck twenty-four equal hours in every season, an hour indifferent to daylight and, for that very reason, convenient for fixing the length of a working day or the term of a loan. Some monastic houses did own water-driven alarms to wake the sacristan, and these may well have contributed the mechanism of the striking train. But the conception of time the tower clocks broadcast, uniform and detached from the sun, was alien to the monastic day the older story assigned them to serve.

In a celebrated essay, a historian of the English working class argued that industrialization replaced the task-oriented rhythms of rural labor, in which a day's work ended when the hay was in, with the abstract discipline of the clock, and that workers experienced the change as a theft. Later scholars have objected that the essay romanticized the preindustrial past, since farm laborers were hired by the day and docked for lateness long before the first mill was built. Yet the more interesting difficulty lies elsewhere.

The essay's own evidence shows workers who were far from oblivious to the clock: their ire was directed less at the measurement of time than at its ownership, and mill masters were accused of setting the factory clock back in the evening and forward in the morning. Workers who could afford pocket watches bought them, in part, to check the master's hours against their own. It might be supposed that such purchases mark a capitulation, the moment at which workers internalized the discipline the essay describes. But a watch bought to audit an employer is a weapon rather than a halter: these workers had accepted that time had a pecuniary value, and what they contested was who would keep the account. To describe their experience as the imposition of clock time is therefore to inflect it in a way that hides how quickly they turned the new order's instruments against the masters who had introduced them.

The average age of the members of the Larkspur Book Club is 61. Teodor, who is 34, concludes that most of the club's members must be much older than he is and that he would almost certainly be its youngest member if he joined.

questions.prompt: The duke's letters to his clockmaker were brief to the point of rudeness, so the man's heirs were astonished to find from the account books how ___ a patron he had been: every invoice was paid early, and each was doubled at the New Year.

explanation.key: The heirs' astonishment sets the curt letters against the account books, which show invoices paid early and doubled: an extremely generous patron, munificent.

distractors.parsimonious: Stingy would match the rude letters, so it would not astonish anyone, and doubled invoices contradict it.
distractors.capricious: Unpredictable; paying early every time and doubling every invoice is consistent, not whimsical.
distractors.negligent: Careless payers do not pay early.
distractors.exacting: Demanding is the trap of 'patron' and the brusque letters, but the account books show generosity, not demands.

questions.prompt: Reviewers who dismissed the young novelist as a mere (i) ___ of the masters she admired were not wrong to notice her borrowings; they were (ii) ___, however, in failing to see that she borrowed in order to quarrel.

explanation.key: (i) 'A mere ___ of the masters she admired', justified by her 'borrowings', is an inferior imitator: epigone. (ii) 'However' turns from what the reviewers got right to what they missed; failing to see her purpose makes them slow to understand: obtuse.

distractors.iconoclast: An attacker of established idols; the reviewers' charge was imitation, not attack, and 'mere' makes it a belittling label.
distractors.detractor: A critic who disparages; she admired the masters, so the reviewers could not call her their detractor.
distractors.lucid: Clear-thinking; praise, but 'failing to see' is a fault.
distractors.discreet: Tactful or reserved (not discrete, separate); tact has nothing to do with failing to grasp her purpose.

questions.prompt: Those who served under the admiral expected a (i) ___, and his first orders, terse and exacting, seemed to confirm the reputation; yet the logbooks show that he regularly chose to (ii) ___ the improvised repairs his officers made without authority, and that the punishments the regulations prescribed he would (iii) ___ so consistently that his crews came to regard the printed scale as a ceiling rather than a rule.

explanation.key: (i) A reputation that terse, exacting orders 'confirm' is that of a strict disciplinarian: martinet. (ii) 'Yet' reverses that expectation, so he approved the unauthorized repairs: sanction in its sense of authorize, not its everyday sense of penalize. (iii) A printed scale that becomes 'a ceiling rather than a rule' means the punishments were regularly reduced below it: temper (moderate), not exact.

distractors.mediator: A go-between; terse, exacting orders would not confirm such a reputation.
distractors.maverick: An unconventional independent; exacting orders confirm strictness, not independence.
distractors.countermand: To revoke an order; what a martinet would do, which is exactly what 'yet' rules out.
distractors.exact: To demand and inflict in full; that would make the printed scale the rule, not a ceiling.
distractors.perpetuate: To keep in existence; it does not explain why the scale came to be seen as an upper limit.
distractors.rescind: To revoke; like countermand, it is what a martinet would do to unauthorized repairs, which 'yet' rules out.

questions.prompt: Collectors burned by the forgery scandal grew ___ of any painting that surfaced without a documented history, refusing even to inspect works their own dealers swore by.
choices: chary
covetous
leery
credulous
gullible
oblivious

explanation.key: Having been 'burned', the collectors would not even look at undocumented works: they became cautious and suspicious, chary and leery.

distractors.credulous: Trap pair with gullible: true synonyms for too ready to believe, the opposite of refusing works dealers swore by.
distractors.gullible: Trap pair with credulous: wrong polarity.
distractors.covetous: Greedy to own; they refused even to inspect the works.
distractors.oblivious: They were acutely aware of the risk, not unaware.

questions.prompt: Historians long treated the water-driven alarm and the weight-driven escapement as successive stages in a single line of development, the second refining the first; the newly dated fragments from the cathedral workshop, however, show the two mechanisms to have been ___, so that neither can have been the other's ancestor.
choices: sequential
contemporaneous
antithetical
successive
coeval
derivative

explanation.key: 'However' reverses 'successive stages', and new dating that rules out descent means the two existed at the same time: contemporaneous and coeval.

distractors.sequential: Trap pair with successive: the old view the 'however' overturns.
distractors.antithetical: Directly opposed; dating says when the mechanisms existed, not that they were opposites.
distractors.derivative: Derived from another; exactly the ancestry the sentence denies.

questions.prompt: The biographer is careful never to ___ the poet in his own voice; the damaging stories are always attributed to her enemies, though he repeats them with a relish that makes his scruple look like a technicality.
choices: exculpate
malign
emulate
absolve
traduce
flatter

explanation.key: The 'scruple' is the thing he avoids doing himself while passing on 'damaging stories' with relish: speaking ill of her. Malign and traduce both mean to slander. The relish makes the scruple a technicality because he gets the slander told without telling it.

distractors.exculpate: Trap pair with absolve: clearing her of blame. Avoiding that in his own voice would be no 'scruple', and it would not be undercut by repeating the damaging stories.
distractors.emulate: To imitate; unrelated to damaging stories.
distractors.flatter: Wrong polarity: the stories are damaging, and declining to flatter is no scruple.

questions.prompt: His rivals took the envoy's endless requests for clarification as proof of a slow mind; only after the treaty was signed did they grasp that he had ___ confusion throughout, having understood the draft better than the clerks who wrote it.
choices: betrayed
feigned
allayed
shammed
manifested
mitigated

explanation.key: He understood the draft better than its authors, so the confusion his rivals saw was not real: he pretended it. Feigned and shammed both mean put on a false show of.

distractors.betrayed: Trap pair with manifested: both mean showed, but they imply the confusion was genuine, which 'having understood the draft better' rules out.
distractors.allayed: Near-pair with mitigated: lessened. The envoy's requests did not reduce anyone's confusion; his rivals were misled, not reassured.

questions.prompt: The author's attitude toward the view of the 'more recent school' of theorists is best described as
choices: unreserved: the view is presented as explaining both why federations endure and how they come to fail
appreciative but critical: the view is credited with explaining a genuine puzzle, though the mechanism it identifies is shown to be capable of undoing what it is said to protect
dismissive: the view is treated as a rationalization of courts' reluctance to enforce the constitutional division of powers
approving of its rejection of judicial enforcement, but doubtful that parties can carry provincial interests into the national capital
favorable on balance, since the view improves on Madison's argument even though it abandons Madison's concern with faction

explanation.key: The author grants 'real explanatory merit' (it accounts for durable federations whose courts rarely strike down statutes) but says it is 'curiously silent about the converse case': the same party discipline can nullify provincial autonomy. That is measured appreciation plus a specific criticism.

distractors.unreserved: the view is presented as exp: Too strong: the author says the view is silent about how the mechanism can fail.
distractors.dismissive: the view is treated as a rat: Wrong polarity: the author credits it with real explanatory merit.
distractors.approving of its rejection of judicial e: Half-right in tone, wrong in content: the view notes that courts enforce sporadically rather than rejecting enforcement, and the author's worry is the reverse, that parties carry the capital's instructions to the provinces.
distractors.favorable on balance, since the view imp: The author never ranks the view against Madison's; the closing point about faction is the author's own correction, not a complaint that the view abandoned Madison.

questions.prompt: Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply. The passage supports which of the following?
choices: A federation in which courts seldom strike down national statutes need not be one in which provincial prerogatives are disregarded.
Provincial autonomy is likely to be more secure where rival parties compete at both levels of government than where a single party commands both.
Madison regarded the propinquity of rulers and ruled as having no political value.

explanation.key: A: Supported. The author grants that the party thesis explains the durability of federations whose courts almost never strike down a national statute: there, parties make national politicians respect provincial prerogatives. B: Supported, by combining the last two sentences. A single dominant party can nullify provincial autonomy, and the safeguards work only while competition keeps any one organization from commanding both levels. C: Not supported, one notch too strong. Madison held that propinquity also breeds faction, which is a cost, not a claim that it has no value.

questions.prompt: In the context in which it appears, “settled” most nearly means
choices: resolved by a compromise between rival hypotheses
established beyond reasonable doubt
made less turbulent
fixed permanently in position
paid in full

explanation.key: The detection, an observation, 'settled that such mergers produce rapid-process elements', in contrast with the earlier 'matter of conjecture' and with what 'remains open'. It established the fact.

distractors.made less turbulent: The sense of settling a liquid or a mind; nothing calmed.
distractors.fixed permanently in position: The sense of settling into place; the question was resolved, not located.
distractors.paid in full: The sense of settling a debt.
distractors.resolved by a compromise between rival h: The sense of settling a dispute by mutual concession; here an observation decided the question outright, and nothing was split between the hypotheses.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that explains why the elements heavier than iron cannot have been made in the way most of the lighter elements forged in stars were made.

explanation.key: The second sentence ('Nearly everything heavier was forged later, in stars, but fusion can carry a star only as far as iron ...') gives the reason: beyond iron, fusion consumes energy instead of releasing it. The third sentence draws the consequence (neutron capture) but gives no reason, and the fourth and fifth describe the two capture processes.

questions.prompt: The transit authority's conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
choices: Most of the county's riders would rather travel on an electric bus than on a diesel bus.
The price of electricity will not rise at any point during the next twelve years.
Electric buses will typically stay in service for roughly as long as the diesel buses they replace.
The authority can afford to buy all of its electric buses at once.
Diesel buses produce more pollution per mile than electric buses do.

explanation.key: The savings are calculated over 'the twelve years a bus typically stays in service', a figure for the diesel buses. If electric buses wore out much sooner, the lower running costs would have less time to make up the higher price. Negated, C breaks the conclusion.

distractors.Most of the county's riders would rather: Rider preference is irrelevant to costs.
distractors.The price of electricity will not rise a: Too strong: modest rises could still leave the electric buses cheaper to run.
distractors.The authority can afford to buy all of i: The plan replaces buses one at a time as they wear out.
distractors.Diesel buses produce more pollution per: Pollution is not part of a cost argument.

questions.prompt: Engineers who had spent years quietly correcting the bridge's design flaws were dismayed to hear the mayor ___ it at the ribbon-cutting as "the most advanced span in the nation", a claim that invited exactly the scrutiny they had hoped to avoid.

explanation.key: Calling the bridge 'the most advanced span in the nation' is a boast, and boasting invites the scrutiny the engineers feared: vaunt.

distractors.belittle: The mayor's quoted words are praise, not disparagement.
distractors.inspect: The mayor made a claim; the scrutiny the claim invites would come from others.
distractors.decommission: Taking the bridge out of service contradicts a ribbon-cutting.
distractors.insure: Nothing about insurance follows from the quoted claim.

questions.prompt: Critics who treat the mottoes cut into old sundials as ornament mistake their makers' priorities: to the men who carved them, an inscription was hardly (i) ___ to the instrument, since a dial that told the hour without (ii) ___ the brevity of life was only half made.

explanation.key: (i) The critics' error is treating the motto as ornament; the makers' view is the reverse, and 'hardly' negates the blank. So the blank must mean ornamental or external: hardly extrinsic, which means essential. The tempting intrinsic gives 'hardly essential', the critics' view. (ii) A dial without its motto was 'only half made', so the full dial had to indicate life's brevity as well as the hour: denoting.

distractors.germane: Relevant; 'hardly germane' would side with the critics.
distractors.intrinsic: The polarity trap: with 'hardly' it says the motto was inessential, which is the critics' mistake, not the makers' view.
distractors.belying: Contradicting; the motto is meant to state life's brevity, not contradict it.
distractors.dismissing: Setting aside as unimportant; the motto exists to insist on life's brevity, so a dial 'without dismissing' it would be the complete one, not the half-made one: the polarity is reversed.

questions.prompt: The poem the nephew wrote in the year of the count's death has always been read as a(n) (i) ___, and the grief in it is real; but the letters show the count to have been a (ii) ___ to his last winter, and the feasts the poem so movingly records him renouncing were never renounced at all. Biographers who mine the poem for the inner man and the letters for the outer, treating them as (iii) ___ sources, miss that the nephew mourned a man the count never was.

explanation.key: (i) A poem written in the year of a death, with real grief in it, is a lament: elegy. (ii) 'But' and the feasts that were 'never renounced at all' show the count kept his pleasures: sybarite. (iii) The biographers split the sources, one for the inner man and one for the outer, so they treat them as separate and non-overlapping: discrete. The final clause says that split is the mistake, because the poem's inner man is a fiction.

distractors.lampoon: A satirical attack; it clashes with 'the grief in it is real'.
distractors.polemic: A controversial argument; it does not fit a poem of mourning.
distractors.recluse: One who withdraws from society; a man who kept feasting was no recluse.
distractors.ascetic: The poem's picture of the count, which the letters disprove; 'but' requires the opposite.
distractors.corroborating: Confirming each other; the poem and letters conflict, and the biographers use them for different halves of the man.
distractors.nebulous: Vague; nothing says the biographers think the sources unclear, only that they split them.

questions.prompt: Outsiders called the astronomers a (i) ___, and meant it to sting; the members, far from being (ii) ___, adopted the word themselves, observing that a society admitting only those trained at a single observatory could hardly object to being called exclusive. Their own scorn they saved for the popularizers, whose books they would (iii) ___ in their lectures and consult, a little guiltily, at home.

explanation.key: (i) The word the members later accept as meaning 'exclusive' is a small, closed group: coterie. (ii) The label was 'meant to sting', and 'far from being ___' they adopted it, so the blank is the stung reaction they did not have: perturbed. (iii) 'Scorn' for the popularizers, contrasted with consulting their books 'guiltily' at home, means they ridiculed the books in public: deride.

distractors.rabble: A disorderly crowd; an insult, but not one a society could accept as meaning 'exclusive'.
distractors.vanguard: Leaders of a movement; a compliment, not a word meant to sting.
distractors.mollified: Soothed; a stinging label cannot soothe, so 'far from being mollified' makes no sense.
distractors.tout: To promote; the opposite of scorn.
distractors.cite: To refer to; this creates no contrast with consulting the books 'guiltily' at home.

questions.prompt: The candidate's answers at the hearing were ___: fluent, confident and endlessly quotable, yet so smooth that afterward no one on the committee could say what he had actually committed to.
choices: glib
faltering
facile
hesitant
candid
terse

explanation.key: Fluent and confident but empty, so smooth that they committed him to nothing: glib and facile, superficially easy speech.

distractors.faltering: Trap pair with hesitant: true synonyms for unsure speech, the opposite of 'fluent, confident'.
distractors.hesitant: Trap pair with faltering: wrong polarity.
distractors.candid: Frank answers would have made his commitments clear.
distractors.terse: 'Endlessly quotable' fluency is not brevity, and terse answers would not be called smooth.

questions.prompt: The boundary dispute the commissioners had hoped to settle in a season outlasted three commissions; it was not that the parties were bitter, for the sessions were unfailingly courteous, but that each concession seemed to generate a fresh claim, so that the dispute remained as ___ at the end as at the start.
choices: acrimonious
intractable
tractable
rancorous
refractory
quiescent

explanation.key: A dispute that outlasted three commissions because every concession produced a new claim stayed resistant to solution: intractable and refractory.

distractors.acrimonious: Trap pair with rancorous: both mean bitter and fit a long dispute, but 'it was not that the parties were bitter' rules them out.
distractors.tractable: Manageable; the opposite of a dispute that outlasted three commissions.
distractors.quiescent: Dormant; fresh claims kept coming, so the dispute was not quiet.

questions.prompt: The letter is remarkable less for its anger than for its restraint: the bishop, who had every reason to be harsh with the young priest, chose instead to ___ him, naming the fault plainly but closing with an invitation to dine.
choices: castigate
admonish
pardon
excoriate
reprove
absolve

explanation.key: 'Instead' of being harsh, yet 'naming the fault plainly', means a firm but mild correction: admonish and reprove.

distractors.castigate: Trap pair with excoriate: severe rebuke, the harshness the bishop chose 'instead' to avoid.
distractors.pardon: Trap pair with absolve: to forgive. But the bishop names the fault plainly, which is a correction, not a release from blame.

questions.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with
choices: defending the traditional view that the episodic form of the picaresque was a defect later corrected by the realist novel
showing that the poverty of the picaresque hero accounts for both the genre's subject matter and its structure
arguing that a revisionist defense of picaresque form rightly rejects one charge but misidentifies the source of the form's coherence
reconciling the traditional and revisionist accounts by showing that each describes a different phase of the genre
demonstrating that Lazarillo de Tormes is better understood as a legal deposition than as a work of fiction

explanation.key: Paragraph 1 states the traditional verdict. Paragraph 2 presents the revisionist defense, credits it with disposing of the 'failure to achieve plot' assumption, then objects that it 'purchases coherence ... by denying them a designer', and puts forward a forensic, narrator-designed coherence instead.

distractors.defending the traditional view that the: Wrong verb: the author accepts that the revisionists disposed of the 'defect' assumption.
distractors.showing that the poverty of the picaresq: That is the revisionist view, which the author qualifies.
distractors.reconciling the traditional and revision: No phases are distinguished; the author corrects both accounts.
distractors.demonstrating that Lazarillo de Tormes i: Extreme: 'forensic' describes the form of the narration; the author never denies the book is fiction.

questions.prompt: The author's argument suggests that the traditional literary historians and the revisionist critics share which of the following assumptions about the early picaresque novel?
choices: Its satire is directed chiefly at the clergy and the nobility.
Its episodic structure should be judged by the standards of the realist novel.
The order and selection of its episodes are not the product of a narrator's deliberate design.
Its hero's poverty is what prevents the episodes from showing development.
Its narrator addresses his story to an imagined reader rather than to a particular person.

explanation.key: Two steps. The traditional account finds no shape ('the book could end almost anywhere'), so it sees no design. The revisionists explain the shape as a mirror of the hero's precarious life, which the author says 'purchases coherence ... by denying them a designer'. Both views leave out the narrator who arranges the episodes, and that narrator is the author's own contribution.

distractors.Its satire is directed chiefly at the cl: The satire's targets are mentioned only in the traditional account, and 'chiefly' is not said.
distractors.Its episodic structure should be judged: Only the traditional view judges it so; the revisionists reject that demand.
distractors.Its hero's poverty is what prevents the: The revisionist explanation; the traditional historians simply fault the form.
distractors.Its narrator addresses his story to an i: Neither group is said to hold this, and the author stresses a particular addressee.

questions.prompt: Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply. According to the passage, the traditional account of the picaresque holds which of the following?
choices: The picaresque made the lives of ordinary and poor people available as material for later fiction.
The picaresque spares the clergy and nobility while exposing the dishonesty of its low-born narrator.
The picaresque hero acquires practical cunning without acquiring wisdom.

explanation.key: A: Yes. The picaresque 'supplied the realist novel with its subject, the ordinary and the poor'. B: No, the relation is reversed: priests, nobles and officials 'prove no more honest than he'. C: Yes. 'The hero learns tricks rather than wisdom' is among the traditional complaints.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A traditional account is stated; a concession about monastic alarms is made; evidence about town clocks is then used to reject the account entirely.

A traditional account is stated; evidence about where early clocks were used is offered against it; a difference in how hours were reckoned is shown to deepen the objection, and a limited monastic contribution is conceded.
Two rival accounts of the clock's origin are presented, and the evidence is shown to favor neither.
A traditional account is stated, evidence against it is presented, and the account is then revised to locate the clock's invention in the towns rather than the monasteries.
A claim about the inaccuracy of early clocks is advanced and then qualified by evidence that monastic alarms kept better time.

explanation.key: Paragraph 1: the monastic-origin commonplace, then the documentary evidence (inaccurate clocks, rare in monastic sources, abundant in town towers). Paragraph 2: equal versus unequal hours makes the gap 'metaphysical', not just one of location; the alarms 'may well have contributed' the striking mechanism (a concession); the conception of time was alien to the monastery.

distractors.A traditional account is stated; a conce: Wrong order, since the concession comes near the end, and 'entirely' ignores that concession.
distractors.Two rival accounts of the clock's origin: The evidence clearly tells against the traditional account.
distractors.A traditional account is stated, evidenc: Half-right: the passage says where clocks appeared in abundance, not where they were invented, and it ends on a conceptual difference, not a relocated invention.
distractors.A claim about the inaccuracy of early cl: The alarms' accuracy is never compared.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the relationship the passage describes between the monastic water-driven alarms and the town clocks?
choices: A navigational instrument designed for ships is later adopted by land surveyors, who use it to fix positions just as sailors did.
A calendar reform introduced by a church is resisted for decades by merchants who prefer the older reckoning of the year.
A mechanical toy built to amuse a court supplies the valve design later used in factory pumps meant to replace human labor, a purpose its builders never contemplated.
A town's clock tower is refitted with a more accurate mechanism but continues to strike the unequal hours of the old offices.
A treatise preserved in a monastery library inspires university scholars, who develop its ideas and acknowledge their debt to it.

explanation.key: The alarms may have 'contributed the mechanism of the striking train', but the conception of time the tower clocks broadcast was 'alien' to the monastic world. The structure is a device passing on its mechanism to a successor whose purpose is foreign to the original's setting. The toy and the pumps match that.

distractors.A navigational instrument designed for s: The purpose carries over unchanged; in the passage the conception does not.
distractors.A calendar reform introduced by a church: A surface match (religious and commercial timekeeping) with no mechanism handed on.
distractors.A town's clock tower is refitted with a: A surface match on clocks; here the old conception survives, the reverse of the passage.
distractors.A treatise preserved in a monastery libr: Ideas are what pass on here, whereas in the passage only the mechanism passed and the idea did not.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that introduces a reading of the workers' conduct that would, if accepted, support the celebrated essay's thesis rather than complicate it.

explanation.key: The sixth sentence ('It might be supposed that such purchases mark a capitulation ...') offers a reading on which buying watches shows workers absorbing the clock discipline imposed on them, which fits the essay's thesis. The next sentence rejects it ('a weapon rather than a halter'). The objection about farm laborers and the evidence about clock-tampering both complicate the thesis rather than support it.

questions.prompt: In the context in which it appears, the phrase “who would keep the account” refers to
choices: who would maintain the mill's financial ledgers
who would set the wage paid for an hour of work
who would control the measurement of the hours that were worked
who would record the history of the workers' grievances
who would be held responsible for time lost to lateness

explanation.key: The account is the reckoning of time itself. Workers had accepted that time had a pecuniary value, and their quarrel was with masters who set the factory clock back and forward, while their watches let them 'check the master's hours against their own'. What they contested was who controlled the measurement of hours worked.

distractors.who would maintain the mill's financial: The literal bookkeeping sense; the dispute was over the clock, not the mill's books.
distractors.who would set the wage paid for an hour: The workers contested the measurement of hours, not the rate paid for them; the passage says they had accepted time's pecuniary value.
distractors.who would record the history of the work: Takes 'account' as a narrative; no one in the passage is writing a history of grievances.
distractors.who would be held responsible for time l: Echoes the earlier docking for lateness, but the sentence concerns who keeps the reckoning, not who bears the penalty.

questions.prompt: The reasoning in Teodor's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: draws conclusions about the ages of most individual members from their average age alone
assumes that the club's membership will not change before Teodor joins
relies on figures about a club that may not be typical of all book clubs
takes for granted that older members prefer different books from younger ones
confuses the ages at which members joined the club with their present ages

explanation.key: An average of 61 is compatible with many members younger than 34, provided a few are much older. Teodor treats the average as telling him about most members and about the youngest one.

distractors.assumes that the club's membership will: A minor point; the conclusion fails even if the membership stays the same.
distractors.relies on figures about a club that may: His conclusion concerns this club only.
distractors.takes for granted that older members pre: The argument says nothing about reading tastes.
distractors.confuses the ages at which members joine: The average age is a present figure, and nothing suggests joining ages.
